Senses.Note: Exact count: 408 hits in 134 texts; lion's roar 558/146 and lion's cave 96/61. One animal/appraisal sense. The phrase “true lion cub” (真師子兒) marks the cub as genuine but does not create another referent; roar, shout, chamber entry, and verse are deployments, not senses.

Occurrences.Kwic: 主曰忝講得經論二十餘本師曰莫是師子兒否主曰不敢師作噓噓聲
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In the Recorded Sayings of the Ancient Worthies (古尊宿語錄), Mazu Daoyi asks a scripture lecturer whether he is a lion cub; the lecturer declines and Mazu hisses.

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧一喝，師云：「真師子兒，善能哮吼。」僧又喝
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In the Recorded Sayings of Master Yushan (雨山和尚語錄), Yushan Shangsi calls a reviewed unnamed participant a true lion cub well able to roar after the participant shouts.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問：如何是師子兒？師曰：毛頭排宇宙。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In the Complete Collection of the Five Lamps, fascicles 1–33 (五燈全書(第1卷-第33卷)), Qingping Weikuang answers the direct question 'what is the lion cub?' by saying that the tips of its hair line up the cosmos.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師子窟中師子兒，哮吼吒沙天地裂。揮拂子曰：呵呵！好大哥
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In the Complete Collection of the Five Lamps, fascicles 34–120 (五燈全書(第34卷-第120卷)), Yinming Lun puts the lion cub in the lion's cave, roaring until heaven and earth split, before waving the whisk.

Occurrences.Kwic: 參禪信得及，休向外邊覓，若真師子兒，豈喫殘羹汁；
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In the Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Xueguan (雪關和尚語錄), Xueguan Zhiyin says in verse that a true lion cub would not eat leftover soup.

Occurrences.Kwic: 山曰：真師子兒，善能哮吼。乃入室受印，依附七年。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In the Complete Collection of the Five Lamps, fascicles 1–33 (五燈全書(第1卷-第33卷)), Jiashan Shanhui calls Huangshan Yuelun a true lion cub able to roar; the record then says Yuelun entered the chamber, received the seal, and remained seven years.

Occurrences.Kwic: 東苑是真師子兒，纔破口吼時，父祖早已喪盡，豈況世間魔乎？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In the Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Huigong Xiong of Nanhai Baoxianglin (南海寶象林慧弓詗禪師語錄), Huigong Xiong calls Dongyuan a true lion cub but says that when Dongyuan opened his mouth to roar, his fathers and ancestors were already lost.

Occurrences.Kwic: 出群湏是英靈漢敵勝還他師子兒選佛若無如是眼假饒千載亦奚為
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Linked-Pearls Collection of Verses on Old Cases (禪宗頌古聯珠通集) preserves the verse without a local byline; parallel lamp commentary attributes its four-line appraisal to Nantang Yuanjing, who says an outstanding person is required to leave the crowd and grants victory to the lion cub.

Senses.Explanation: A lion cub is a young lion. Chan records repeatedly bend this animal image into a public test-name and appraisal for a person. Mazu asks a lecturer who boasts of expounding many texts, “are you not a lion cub?”; after the lecturer declines the name, Mazu makes a hissing sound and the exchange continues. Named teachers say “a true lion cub, well able to roar” (真師子兒，善能哮吼) after a reviewed unnamed participant shouts or answers; in one lineage narrative this appraisal is followed by entering the chamber and receiving the seal. A direct question, “what is the lion cub?” receives “the tips of its hair line up the cosmos” (毛頭排宇宙). Formal verse places the cub in the lion's cave roaring until heaven and earth split, while another warning says that a true lion cub does not eat leftover soup. Later commentary can sharpen or contest an appraisal, saying that when Dongyuan opened his mouth to roar his fathers and ancestors were already lost. The Zen-specific bend is the recurrent use of the young lion as an explicit name given, refused, tested, and confirmed in encounters, often by the observable ability to roar. The entry does not infer succession whenever the words occur.
